source_metadata.title: The Successful Application of a Heparin Nomogram in a Community Hospital

atoms.canonical_statement: The study evaluated whether a heparin nomogram in two community hospitals improved anticoagulation control and reduced hospital length of stay.
The analyzed cohort comprised 163 hospitalized patients with a primary diagnosis of DVT or PE: 82 prenomogram and 81 postnomogram.

population.label: Hospitalized patients with a primary diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism at Sudbury General Hospital or Memorial Hospital
inclusion_criteria: Primary diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: The study used a retrospective historical before-and-after design comparing a prenomogram period before April 1993 with a postnomogram period after June 1993; April-June 1993 was excluded as a familiarization interval.

Postnomogram patients received an initial 5000-IU heparin bolus followed by continuous infusion of 20,000 U in 500 mL of 5% dextrose; initial infusion was 1680 U/h for low bleeding risk and 1280 U/h for high bleeding risk.

exposures.details: Continuous infusion 20,000 U in 500 mL D5W; initial rate 1680 U/h if low bleeding risk or 1280 U/h if high bleeding risk.

atoms.canonical_statement: The first APTT was measured 6 hours after the bolus, after which nurses adjusted the infusion using the heparin nomogram.

exposures.details: Postnomogram management after the April-June 1993 implementation/familiarization period in two community hospitals.

atoms.canonical_statement: For an APTT of <50 seconds, the nomogram instructed staff to give a 5000-U heparin bolus, do not stop the infusion, increase the infusion by 3 mL/h, and repeat APTT 6 hours later.

exposures.details: Postnomogram management after the April-June 1993 implementation/familiarization period in two community hospitals.

atoms.canonical_statement: For an APTT of 50-59 seconds, the nomogram instructed staff to give no bolus, do not stop the infusion, increase the infusion by 3 mL/h, and repeat APTT 6 hours later.

exposures.details: Postnomogram management after the April-June 1993 implementation/familiarization period in two community hospitals.

atoms.canonical_statement: For an APTT of 60-85 seconds, the nomogram instructed staff to give no bolus, do not stop the infusion, make no rate change, and repeat APTT the next morning.

exposures.details: Postnomogram management after the April-June 1993 implementation/familiarization period in two community hospitals.

atoms.canonical_statement: For an APTT of 86-95 seconds, the nomogram instructed staff to give no bolus, do not stop the infusion, decrease the infusion by 2 mL/h, and repeat APTT the next morning.

exposures.details: Postnomogram management after the April-June 1993 implementation/familiarization period in two community hospitals.

atoms.canonical_statement: For an APTT of 96-120 seconds, the nomogram instructed staff to give no bolus, stop the infusion for 30 minutes, decrease the infusion by 2 mL/h, and repeat APTT 6 hours later.

exposures.details: Postnomogram management after the April-June 1993 implementation/familiarization period in two community hospitals.

atoms.canonical_statement: For an APTT of >120 seconds, the nomogram instructed staff to give no bolus, stop the infusion for 60 minutes, decrease the infusion by 4 mL/h, and repeat APTT 4 hours later.

exposures.details: Postnomogram management after the April-June 1993 implementation/familiarization period in two community hospitals.

atoms.canonical_statement: The nomogram specified that a physician should be called if APTT was greater than 120 seconds or less than 50 seconds on two consecutive blood samples.

atoms.canonical_statement: The prenomogram comparator was historical physician-directed heparin management before protocol implementation.

exposures.details: Historical control period before April 1993.

atoms.canonical_statement: Use of the nomogram was not mandatory, so the study evaluated real-world effectiveness rather than enforced protocol efficacy.
Warfarin prescribing was left to the treating physician and was not part of the heparin nomogram.
The predefined primary outcome was hospital length of stay.
A secondary outcome was time from initiation of heparin therapy to therapeutic APTT.
A secondary outcome was the frequency with which APTT results fell outside the therapeutic range.

concept.text: APTT result relative to therapeutic window

atoms.canonical_statement: Data validity was assessed by duplicate review of a random sample of 25 charts and intraclass correlation coefficients for major outcomes.

Analyses used chi-square tests for categorical data, unpaired two-tailed t tests for continuous data, odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and Kaplan-Meier/Mantel-Haenszel time-to-event analysis; P<.01 was the significance threshold because multiple tests were performed.
The sample-size calculation targeted approximately 75-80 patients per group to detect a 2-day difference in hospital length of stay with beta 0.8 using a two-tailed test.
Baseline demographic characteristics, diagnoses, comorbidity, and time to warfarin initiation were generally similar between groups.
Inter-rater agreement for hospital length of stay was ICC 0.75.

atoms.canonical_statement: Use of historical controls could have biased the comparison between prenomogram and postnomogram periods.
Other interventions may have differed between the historical study periods, although the authors did not identify a major differing cointervention.
The sample size was insufficient to determine whether the nomogram reduced rare outcomes such as death or hemorrhagic complications.
Because nomogram use was not mandatory and some physicians remained reluctant to use it, the observed effect may not represent full protocol adherence.
The nomogram did not specify discharge criteria or warfarin-transition recommendations, limiting its ability to influence hospital length of stay.

The authors concluded that a heparin nomogram could be used successfully in a community hospital without a structured hematology-thrombosis service, achieving therapeutic anticoagulation faster and more consistently.
The authors concluded that additional measures, potentially including a structured warfarin protocol, would be needed to reduce hospital length of stay.
The project was jointly funded by the Sudbury Memorial Foundation and the Sudbury General Hospital.

extraction_limitations: No DOI, PMID, or other stable bibliographic identifier was printed in the evaluated PDF; none was invented.

The Results prose reports mean time to first therapeutic APTT as 17.8 h, whereas Table 4 and the abstract report 17.9 h; the table value (17.9 h) is used in the corresponding atom and the discrepancy is retained here.
No numeric adverse-event counts were reported in the text available for extraction; no adverse_event atom was fabricated.
The paper is from 1995; atoms record the historical source and should not be interpreted as current dosing guidance.
